nameStory: The wedgeclam gets its name from its distinctive triangular shell shape that looks just like a wooden wedge used for splitting logs. When viewed from the side, these clams form a perfect wedge profile that's unmistakable once you know what to look for.
description: The wedgeclam is a medium-sized marine bivalve that lives buried in sandy beaches along New England's coast. These clams have thick, sturdy shells that typically measure 2-4 inches across and are shaped like a triangle or wedge when viewed from the side. Their shells are usually cream to yellowish-white in color, sometimes with faint growth rings visible on the surface. Unlike many other clams, wedgeclams prefer the high-energy surf zone where waves crash onto sandy shores.

idTips.label: Triangular shell shape
idTips.description: The shell forms a distinct wedge or triangle when viewed from the side - thick and tall at one end, tapering to thin at the other, feeling solid and heavy in your hand

idTips.label: Smooth, thick shell
idTips.description: Shell surface feels smooth to the touch with a chalky texture, much thicker and sturdier than typical clam shells, often with a slight sheen

idTips.label: Size and weight
idTips.description: Noticeably heavy for their size (2-4 inches), with a solid, dense feel that distinguishes them from hollow-feeling surf clams

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Cream to pale yellow exterior, sometimes with faint concentric growth rings that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Beach zone location
idTips.description: Found in the active surf zone of sandy beaches, often partially buried where waves are actively washing over them

habitat: Wedgeclams live in clean, sandy beaches along New England's open coastline, particularly where there's active wave action and surf. They prefer the intertidal zone and shallow subtidal areas with medium to coarse sand, often found on beaches exposed to the Atlantic Ocean rather than in protected bays or muddy areas. Look for them on beaches like those found on Cape Cod, the New Hampshire seacoast, and Maine's sandy stretches.

seasonality.spring: Live clams begin moving closer to shore as waters warm, and empty shells wash up on beaches after winter storms. This is an excellent time to find fresh, intact shells.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding live specimens in shallow water during low tide, when they're most active and closest to the surface. Shells collected now often show the freshest coloration.
seasonality.fall: Clams start moving to deeper water, but storms often wash up many shells on beaches. Fall storms can reveal large numbers of weathered shells.
seasonality.winter: Live clams retreat to deeper water, but winter storms frequently deposit shells on beaches. Shells found now are often bleached white and worn smooth by wave action.

funFact: Wedgeclams are like the surfers of the clam world - they actually prefer living in the crashing surf zone where most other clams would be pummeled to pieces, using their wedge shape to cut through the turbulent sand and water like a natural surfboard.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with surf clams, but wedgeclams are much heavier, more triangular, and have thicker shells. Memory trick: 'Wedge = weighty' - if it feels surprisingly heavy for its size and has that triangular wedge shape, it's a wedgeclam.
contextualKnowledge: Note: This species information should be verified, as wedgeclams (Mesodesma arctatum) may have limited confirmed presence in New England waters, and much of the available information comes from populations in other regions. Always cross-reference local field guides for the most accurate regional information.
compareHints: Since this is the only Mesodesma species typically found in New England waters, compare it with surf clams and quahogs. Unlike thin-shelled surf clams, wedgeclams are much thicker and heavier. Unlike round quahogs, wedgeclams have that distinctive triangular profile and prefer sandy surf zones rather than muddy bays.
